## Next-Token Computation {#sec-vol3-processor-autoregressive}

When a software engineer invokes an LLM through an API call such as `response = client.chat.completions.create(...)`, the interface presents the illusion of a standard remote function call: the client sends a staged prompt string, waits for processing, and receives a completed text response. To someone trained on traditional database query engines or compiler pipelines, it is tempting to imagine that the accelerator compiles the prompt into an internal query plan and executes an end-to-end routine that outputs the entire response buffer in a single atomic pass.

The physical reality on accelerator silicon is fundamentally different. If an inference server receives a $2{,}000$-token prompt, its accelerator can process all $2{,}000$ tokens simultaneously during initial prefill in under 50 milliseconds. Yet generating a mere $200$-token response from that prompt often requires 3 to 5 seconds—nearly two orders of magnitude longer per token.

This stark performance asymmetry stems from a foundational architectural constraint: an accelerator executing a large language model is not an atomic function evaluator, but an *autoregressive sequence continuation engine*. It generates candidate sequences one token at a time through an iterative, loop-carried execution cycle. Understanding this execution cycle is essential for systems engineers designing high-throughput serving runtimes, agent control planes, and latency-sensitive user interfaces.

### Autoregressive Factorization and the Causal Loop

The mathematical principle governing foundation model generation is **autoregressive causal factorization**. Given an input prompt consisting of $M$ staged tokens $\mathbf{x} = (x_1, \dots, x_M)$, the model defines a probability distribution over an output continuation $\mathbf{y}_{1:K} = (y_1, \dots, y_K)$ by decomposing the joint sequence probability using the chain rule of probability:

$$P(\mathbf{y}_{1:K} \mid \mathbf{x}) = \prod_{t=1}^K P(y_t \mid \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}_{<t})$$ {#eq-autoregressive-factorization}

where $\mathbf{y}_{<t} = (y_1, \dots, y_{t-1})$ represents the generated prefix prior to step $t$, with $\mathbf{y}_{<1} = \emptyset$.[^fn-autoregressive-factorization]

[^fn-autoregressive-factorization]: **Autoregressive Factorization** (Statistical Sequence Modeling): The mathematical decomposition of a joint probability distribution over a discrete sequence into an ordered product of conditional univariate distributions. In transformer serving systems, this factorization imposes an absolute sequential dependency on generation: no output token can be evaluated until all preceding tokens have been materialized. \index{Autoregressive Factorization}\index{Inference Engine!Autoregressive Decoding}

This factorization imposes an inescapable, loop-carried data dependency: the probability distribution for token $y_t$ depends strictly on the exact token chosen at step $t-1$:

$$\text{Dependency}(y_t) = \{\mathbf{x}, y_1, y_2, \dots, y_{t-2}, y_{t-1}\}$$ {#eq-decode-dependency}

To appreciate the systems implications of this dependency, contrast the autoregressive loop with the execution model of a classical superscalar out-of-order CPU (such as an Intel x86-64 or ARM Neoverse core). In a modern CPU pipeline, hardware schedulers leverage *Instruction-Level Parallelism* (ILP): if instruction $B$ does not depend on the register outputs of instruction $A$, hardware register renaming and reservation stations can dispatch both instructions concurrently across parallel execution ports. When branches occur, branch predictors allow the CPU to speculatively execute dozens of instructions ahead of the current program counter.

In an autoregressive language model, however, no such speculative shortcut exists along a single sequence trajectory. The model cannot compute step 50 before step 49 has been sampled, because the continuous hidden activation vector at step 50 is an attention-weighted combination over the Key and Value representations of all previous tokens—including token 49. Every output token requires a distinct, sequential forward pass through the entire neural network.

The contrast between prompt ingestion (*prefill*) and response generation (*decode*) illustrates this boundary:

- **Prefill (Parallel Computation):** During prompt ingestion, all $M$ prompt tokens are known in advance. The accelerator evaluates all $M$ positions concurrently within a single forward pass as an $M \times d_{\text{model}}$ matrix-matrix multiplication (GEMM). To prevent earlier tokens from attending to later tokens, the attention mechanism applies an upper-triangular *causal attention mask* $\mathbf{M}_{\text{causal}}$:
  $$\mathbf{M}_{\text{causal}}(i, j) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } j \le i \\ -\infty & \text{if } j > i \end{cases}$$ {#eq-causal-mask}
  Because $-\infty$ evaluates to zero after exponentiation in the attention softmax ($e^{-\infty} = 0$), position $i$ receives attention weight only from positions $j \le i$.[^fn-causal-masking] Because all $M$ tokens are processed together, the model weights loaded into accelerator SRAM can be reused across all $M$ tokens. This high arithmetic intensity (FLOPs per byte transferred) fully saturates parallel tensor cores, making prefill compute-bound.
- **Decode (Serial Iteration):** During generation, spatial parallelism collapses along the trajectory dimension. Generating $K$ tokens requires launching $K$ successive forward passes across the accelerator bus. Each step evaluates only a single token vector ($1 \times d_{\text{model}}$) through a matrix-vector multiplication (GEMV). Because generating that single token requires streaming all tens of gigabytes of model parameters from High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) into on-chip cache, arithmetic intensity collapses to near zero. Generation becomes strictly memory-bandwidth bound: the tensor cores sit mostly idle, waiting on the physical speed of the memory bus.

[^fn-causal-masking]: **Causal Masking** (Transformer Architecture): An upper-triangular masking matrix enforced in self-attention layers that zeros out attention weights from subsequent sequence positions. This ensures that during parallel training and prefill, positions can only incorporate information from preceding context, strictly preserving the autoregressive property. \index{Causal Masking}\index{Attention!Causal Mask}

### The Iterative Serving Execution Cycle

Because the neural core possesses no autonomous program counter, it cannot drive its own iteration. When an accelerator finishes a single forward pass, it evaluates the final layer's *unembedding projection*—multiplying the final hidden activation vector $\mathbf{h}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}}$ by unembedding weight matrix $\mathbf{W}_U \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}| \times d_{\text{model}}}$—to yield a vector of raw, unnormalized scores called **logits** $\mathbf{z}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|}$:

$$\mathbf{z}_t = \mathbf{W}_U \mathbf{h}_t = f_\Theta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}_{<t})$$ {#eq-forward-step}

where $|\mathcal{V}|$ is the vocabulary cardinality (typically $32{,}000$ to $128{,}000$ distinct token identifiers).

At this exact moment, accelerator silicon execution halts. The GPU hardware does not pick the next token, does not append characters to an output string, and does not advance an instruction pointer. It simply deposits the float logit vector $\mathbf{z}_t$ into device High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM).

To advance generation, an external host software process—the *inference serving engine* (such as vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, or llama.cpp)—must supervise an explicit 4-phase execution cycle (@fig-autoregressive-loop):

1. **Forward Evaluation:** The serving engine dispatches compute kernels to evaluate $f_\Theta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}_{<t})$ on the accelerator, producing logit vector $\mathbf{z}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|}$.
2. **Decoding and Sampling:** A sampling kernel transforms raw logits $\mathbf{z}_t$ into an emission distribution $Q(y_t)$ and draws a discrete token identifier $\hat{y}_t \in \mathcal{V}$.
3. **State Mutation:** The serving daemon escrows token $\hat{y}_t$ in host memory and commits its corresponding Key and Value projection vectors into the accelerator's Key-Value (KV) cache (@sec-vol3-processor-tokenization), ensuring previous attention states do not need to be recomputed on subsequent iterations.
4. **Predicate Verification:** The host runtime tests whether sequence generation should terminate by evaluating the halt predicate:
   $$\text{Halt}(t) \iff \text{SuffixMatch}(\mathbf{y}_{\le t}, \mathcal{S}_{\text{stop}}) \lor (t \ge K_{\max})$$ {#eq-halt-predicate}
   where $\mathcal{S}_{\text{stop}} \subset \mathcal{V}^*$ denotes a set of terminal delimiter sequences and $K_{\max}$ represents the maximum token step ceiling configured by the host agent runtime.

::: {#fig-autoregressive-loop fig-cap="**Autoregressive Serialization Loop**: Causal dependency chain across the inference serving daemon and accelerator neural core during iterative token decoding." fig-alt="Autoregressive serialization loop illustrating the four-phase boundary between the inference daemon and the neural core."}
![](images/svg/autoregressive_serialization_loop.svg){width="100%"}
:::

In software, this 4-phase execution cycle is implemented directly within the inference service daemon's engine loop. @lst-autoregressive-decode-loop illustrates a production-style serving loop in Python, demonstrating how the host runtime drives the accelerator, mutates state, and enforces stop conditions.

::: {#lst-autoregressive-decode-loop lst-cap="**Autoregressive Generation Loop**: Python implementation executing the four-phase serving cycle across the inference daemon and accelerator boundary."}
```python
def autoregressive_decode(model, prompt_tokens, stop_tokens, max_new_tokens=512, tau=0.7):
    """Iterative serving loop across the 4-phase execution cycle."""
    tokens = list(prompt_tokens)
    
    # Phase 0: Prefill prompt tokens and initialize KV cache
    logits, kv_cache = model.prefill(tokens)

    for step in range(max_new_tokens):
        # Phase 1 & 2: Forward evaluation and logit sampling
        probs = softmax(logits / max(tau, 1e-5))
        next_token = sample_categorical(probs)  # argmax if tau -> 0
        tokens.append(next_token)

        # Phase 3: State mutation (append token KV vectors to accelerator cache)
        logits, kv_cache = model.decode_step(next_token, kv_cache)

        # Phase 4: Predicate verification (evaluate halt condition)
        if next_token in stop_tokens or matches_stop_suffix(tokens):
            break

    return tokens
```
:::

Notice the suffix-matching logic in Phase 4 of @lst-autoregressive-decode-loop. Because Byte-Pair Encoding splits text based on statistical byte entropy rather than syntax rules (@sec-vol3-processor-tokenization), a multi-character stop delimiter such as `"\nObservation:"` or `"```"` can be fractured across multiple subword token IDs. For instance, the token following a newline may incorporate the first few letters of the delimiter (such as token `"Obs"`), while subsequent letters form another token (`"ervation"`). Consequently, an inference engine cannot rely solely on checking individual token IDs against a static set of integer scalars. It must maintain a rolling suffix buffer of recently decoded characters, verifying whether the tail of the emitted string matches any configured stop delimiter $\mathcal{S}_{\text{stop}}$.

### Reshaping Probability on the Vocabulary Simplex

The raw logits $\mathbf{z}_t = f_\Theta(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}_{<t})$ produced by the neural core define the model's base parameter distribution via the standard softmax function:

$$P_\Theta(y_t = v \mid \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}_{<t}) = \frac{\exp(z_{t, v})}{\sum_{w \in \mathcal{V}} \exp(z_{t, w})}$$ {#eq-base-parameter-likelihood}

However, inference serving engines rarely sample directly from this raw distribution. Instead, the serving runtime reshapes $\mathbf{z}_t$ through a **decoding policy** parameterized by an execution tuple:[^fn-sampling-transforms]

$$\Pi_{\text{sample}} = \langle \tau, k, p, \alpha_{\text{rep}}, \alpha_{\text{pres}}, \alpha_{\text{freq}}, \mathbf{b}, \sigma \rangle$$ {#eq-sampling-policy-tuple}

where $\tau$ is softmax temperature, $k$ is the top-$k$ truncation threshold, $p$ is the nucleus (top-$p$) cumulative probability threshold, $\alpha_{\text{rep}}$ is the repetition penalty, $\alpha_{\text{pres}}$ and $\alpha_{\text{freq}}$ are presence and frequency penalties, $\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|}$ is an additive logit bias vector, and $\sigma \in \mathbb{Z}^+$ is the pseudo-random number generator (PRNG) seed.

[^fn-sampling-transforms]: **Sampling Transformation** (Runtime Decoding Policy): The algorithmic modification of raw neural network logits into an operational emission distribution on the probability simplex. Managed entirely by the host serving runtime without altering underlying parameter weights $\Theta$, the decoding policy governs the trade-off between modal determinism and stochastic diversity. \index{Sampling Transformation}\index{Inference Engine!Decoding Policy}

This sampling pipeline maps raw unnormalized scores into an **emission distribution** $Q(y_t \mid \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}_{<t}; \Pi_{\text{sample}})$ residing on the probability simplex $\Delta^{|\mathcal{V}|-1}$ (the mathematical space of categorical probability distributions where all elements are non-negative and sum to $1.0$):

$$\Delta^{|\mathcal{V}|-1} = \left\{ \mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|} \;\middle|\; \sum_{v=1}^{|\mathcal{V}|} q_v = 1, \; q_v \ge 0 \right\}$$ {#eq-prob-simplex}

The transformation executes across five sequential stages:

1. **Repetition and Frequency Attenuation:** The runtime tracks token occurrence frequencies $c_v(t) = \sum_{j=1}^{t-1} \mathbb{I}(y_j = v)$ within the generated prefix. It applies multiplicative attenuation ($\alpha_{\text{rep}} \ge 1.0$) to penalize tokens that have already been emitted, suppressing repetitive loops:
   $$z'_{t, v} = \begin{cases} z_{t, v} / \alpha_{\text{rep}} & \text{if } c_v(t) > 0 \text{ and } z_{t, v} > 0 \\ z_{t, v} \cdot \alpha_{\text{rep}} & \text{if } c_v(t) > 0 \text{ and } z_{t, v} \le 0 \\ z_{t, v} & \text{if } c_v(t) = 0 \end{cases}$$ {#eq-repetition-penalty}
   Notice the sign-dependent branching in @eq-repetition-penalty: if a previously emitted token has a positive logit ($z > 0$), dividing by $\alpha_{\text{rep}} > 1.0$ reduces its score toward zero. If its logit is negative ($z \le 0$), multiplying by $\alpha_{\text{rep}}$ drives it further negative (for example, $-2.0 \times 1.2 = -2.4$), ensuring that repeated tokens are consistently suppressed regardless of logit sign. Additive presence and frequency offsets are then applied:
   $$z''_{t, v} = z'_{t, v} - \alpha_{\text{pres}} \cdot \mathbb{I}(c_v(t) > 0) - \alpha_{\text{freq}} \cdot c_v(t)$$ {#eq-additive-penalties}

2. **Logit Biasing:** An additive bias vector $\mathbf{b} \in [-\infty, +\infty)^{|\mathcal{V}|}$ inflates or suppresses specific token coordinates. Setting $b_v = -\infty$ strictly forbids token $v$ from being selected, a mechanism leveraged by grammar-constrained decoding engines (@sec-vol3-processor-grammar-constrained):
   $$z'''_{t, v} = z''_{t, v} + b_v$$ {#eq-logit-biasing}

3. **Thermal Simplex Scaling:** Logits are scaled by temperature $\tau \in (0, \infty)$:[^fn-softmax-temperature]
   $$\tilde{z}_{t, v} = \frac{z'''_{t, v}}{\tau}$$ {#eq-thermal-scaling}
   Borrowing from the Boltzmann distribution in statistical mechanics, modulating $\tau$ controls entropy on the probability simplex (@fig-temperature-simplex):
   - **Greedy Limit ($\tau \to 0^+$):** Thermal noise approaches zero, collapsing probability mass entirely onto the mode with the maximum logit:
     $$\lim_{\tau \to 0^+} Q(y_t = v \mid \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}_{<t}) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } v = \arg\max_{w \in \mathcal{V}} z'''_{t, w} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$ {#eq-greedy-limit}
     (subject to floating-point drift in GPU parallel reduction trees[^fn-float-determinism]).
   - **Balanced Sampling ($0.2 \le \tau \le 0.8$):** Provides smooth exploration while retaining modal preference.
   - **High-Entropy Limit ($\tau \to \infty$):** High thermal noise washes away differences between logits, dispersing probability mass toward a uniform distribution:
     $$\lim_{\tau \to \infty} Q(y_t = v \mid \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}_{<t}) = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}|}$$ {#eq-uniform-limit}

[^fn-softmax-temperature]: **Temperature Scaling** (Statistical Mechanics / Logit Calibration): A dispersion parameter $\tau$ that scales logit magnitudes prior to the softmax transformation. Derived from statistical mechanics ($P(E) \propto e^{-E / k_B T}$), temperature modulates the sharpness or entropy of the resulting categorical distribution without changing the rank order of candidate tokens. \index{Temperature Scaling}\index{Sampling!Temperature}

[^fn-float-determinism]: **Floating-Point Non-Determinism** (GPU Reduction Trees): In parallel GPU reduction kernels, floating-point addition is non-associative: $(a + b) + c \neq a + (b + c)$. Variations in thread scheduling, warp arrival order, or block sizes across runs can alter the least significant bits of logit values, occasionally causing ties or near-ties to flip even under greedy sampling ($\tau=0$). \index{IEEE 754!Non-Associative Addition}\index{Determinism!Floating-Point Drift}

::: {#fig-temperature-simplex fig-cap="**Thermal Scaling on the Probability Simplex**: Softmax temperature modulation across greedy collapse, balanced sampling, and uniform entropy limits." fig-alt="Thermal scaling of logit distributions on the vocabulary simplex, showing greedy collapse, balanced sampling, and uniform entropy limits."}
![](images/svg/temperature_simplex_scaling.svg){width="100%"}
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Worked Example: Tracing the Softmax Temperature Transformation on a 3-Token Logit Vector"}

**Problem**:
Consider an inference serving engine evaluating candidate next-token continuations for an autonomous agent executing administrative scripts. At decode step $t$, the neural core outputs raw logits $\mathbf{z} = [2.0, 1.0, 0.0]$ across a toy 3-token vocabulary $\mathcal{V} = \{v_1, v_2, v_3\}$ representing candidate bash actions `["read", "write", "delete"]`. Assume no repetition penalties or additive logit biases ($z''' = z$).

Calculate the normalized probability distribution $Q(y)$ under three distinct runtime temperature configurations:
1. Low temperature / greedy sharpening ($\tau = 0.2$)
2. Baseline temperature ($\tau = 1.0$)
3. High temperature / entropy dispersion ($\tau = 2.0$)

Show step-by-step arithmetic and contrast the resulting systems implications for agent execution.

**Solution**:
For each temperature setting $\tau$, compute the scaled logits $\tilde{z}_i = z_i / \tau$, exponentiate each element $e^{\tilde{z}_i}$, calculate normalization sum $Z = \sum_{i=1}^3 e^{\tilde{z}_i}$, and compute final probabilities $P(v_i) = e^{\tilde{z}_i} / Z$.

*Case 1: Low Temperature ($\tau = 0.2$)*
- Scaled logits: $\tilde{\mathbf{z}} = [2.0 / 0.2, 1.0 / 0.2, 0.0 / 0.2] = [10.0, 5.0, 0.0]$
- Exponentials: $e^{10.0} \approx 22{,}026.47$, $e^{5.0} \approx 148.41$, $e^{0.0} = 1.00$
- Normalization sum: $Z = 22{,}026.47 + 148.41 + 1.00 = 22{,}175.88$
- Probabilities:
  $$P(v_1) = \frac{22{,}026.47}{22{,}175.88} \approx 0.9933 \quad (99.33\%)$$
  $$P(v_2) = \frac{148.41}{22{,}175.88} \approx 0.0067 \quad (0.67\%)$$
  $$P(v_3) = \frac{1.00}{22{,}175.88} \approx 0.000045 \quad (0.005\%)$$

*Case 2: Baseline Temperature ($\tau = 1.0$)*
- Scaled logits: $\tilde{\mathbf{z}} = [2.0 / 1.0, 1.0 / 1.0, 0.0 / 1.0] = [2.0, 1.0, 0.0]$
- Exponentials: $e^{2.0} \approx 7.389$, $e^{1.0} \approx 2.718$, $e^{0.0} = 1.000$
- Normalization sum: $Z = 7.389 + 2.718 + 1.000 = 11.107$
- Probabilities:
  $$P(v_1) = \frac{7.389}{11.107} \approx 0.6652 \quad (66.52\%)$$
  $$P(v_2) = \frac{2.718}{11.107} \approx 0.2447 \quad (24.47\%)$$
  $$P(v_3) = \frac{1.000}{11.107} \approx 0.0900 \quad (9.00\%)$$

*Case 3: High Temperature ($\tau = 2.0$)*
- Scaled logits: $\tilde{\mathbf{z}} = [2.0 / 2.0, 1.0 / 2.0, 0.0 / 2.0] = [1.0, 0.5, 0.0]$
- Exponentials: $e^{1.0} \approx 2.718$, $e^{0.5} \approx 1.649$, $e^{0.0} = 1.000$
- Normalization sum: $Z = 2.718 + 1.649 + 1.000 = 5.367$
- Probabilities:
  $$P(v_1) = \frac{2.718}{5.367} \approx 0.5065 \quad (50.65\%)$$
  $$P(v_2) = \frac{1.649}{5.367} \approx 0.3072 \quad (30.72\%)$$
  $$P(v_3) = \frac{1.000}{5.367} \approx 0.1863 \quad (18.63\%)$$

The comparative numerical shifts are summarized in @tbl-temperature-modulation:

| Token Candidate | Raw Logit $z_i$ | $\tau=0.2$ Prob ($Q$) | $\tau=1.0$ Prob ($Q$) | $\tau=2.0$ Prob ($Q$) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $v_1$ (`"read"`) | $2.0$ | **$99.33\%$** | **$66.52\%$** | **$50.65\%$** |
| $v_2$ (`"write"`) | $1.0$ | $0.67\%$ | $24.47\%$ | $30.72\%$ |
| $v_3$ (`"delete"`) | $0.0$ | $0.005\%$ | $9.00\%$ | $18.63\%$ |
: **Softmax temperature probability modulation**: Reshaping candidate token probabilities across greedy sharpening ($\tau=0.2$), baseline ($\tau=1.0$), and high entropy ($\tau=2.0$). {#tbl-temperature-modulation}

**Systems insight**:
At $\tau = 0.2$, dividing logits by a fraction scales their differences by $5\times$, exponentially crushing runner-up candidates and concentrating $99.33\%$ of the probability mass onto modal token $v_1$. In production agent runtimes executing deterministic tasks (such as emitting structured JSON or invoking strict tool schemas), setting $\tau \to 0$ suppresses sampling variance and eliminates syntax errors.

At $\tau = 1.0$, the distribution mirrors the training distribution, but presents a cumulative $33.47\%$ chance of diverging from the mode. At $\tau = 2.0$, dividing logits by $2.0$ compresses score differences by half. Thermal entropy disperses probability mass toward the uniform distribution ($33.3\%$ per token), giving the destructive command $v_3$ (`"delete"`) an $18.63\%$ execution probability despite its lowest raw score. For this reason, agent runtimes strictly gate temperature based on task criticality, refusing elevated temperatures during tool-calling phases.

:::

4. **Support Truncation Filtering:** Restricts candidate selection to active subset $\mathcal{V}_{\text{active}} \subseteq \mathcal{V}$ via top-$k$ truncation:
   $$\mathcal{V}^{(k)} = \operatorname{argtopk}_{v \in \mathcal{V}}(\tilde{z}_{t, v}, k)$$ {#eq-topk-truncation}
   or nucleus (top-$p$) filtering:
   $$\mathcal{V}^{(p)} = \arg\min_{\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathcal{V}^{(k)}} \left\{ |\mathcal{U}| \;\middle|\; \sum_{u \in \mathcal{U}} \frac{\exp(\tilde{z}_{t, u})}{\sum_{w \in \mathcal{V}^{(k)}} \exp(\tilde{z}_{t, w})} \ge p \right\}$$ {#eq-nucleus-truncation}
   masking coordinates outside $\mathcal{V}_{\text{active}} = \mathcal{V}^{(p)}$ to $-\infty$. In algorithmic terms, nucleus filtering sorts candidate tokens by descending probability, computes their cumulative sum, and selects the minimal prefix of tokens whose cumulative probability meets or exceeds threshold $p$, masking all remaining tokens. Top-$k$ sets a hard ceiling on the number of candidate tokens, whereas nucleus (top-$p$) dynamically adjusts the candidate pool size based on the model's confidence, expanding the pool when uncertain and contracting it to a few tokens when confident.

5. **Categorical Draw with PRNG Seeding:** Normalizing active logits yields the final emission distribution:
   $$Q(y_t = v \mid \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}_{<t}; \Pi_{\text{sample}}) = \begin{cases} \frac{\exp(\tilde{z}_{t, v})}{\sum_{u \in \mathcal{V}_{\text{active}}} \exp(\tilde{z}_{t, u})} & \text{if } v \in \mathcal{V}_{\text{active}} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$ {#eq-emission-distribution}
   The sampled token $\hat{y}_t \sim Q$ is drawn via a pseudo-random number generator initialized with seed $\sigma$.

Crucially, the emission distribution $Q(y_t)$ is a mutable Tier 2 software configuration managed by the inference host runtime; the underlying parameter distribution $P_\Theta(y_t)$ is an immutable Tier 3 physical property baked into accelerator weights. An engineer can alter temperature, top-$p$, or logit biases on a per-request basis without modifying a single weight on the accelerator.

If the serving engine repeatedly executes this loop and produces a fluent, high-probability sequence of tokens, what does that establish about the real system? Does high statistical likelihood under the model's parameters guarantee that the generated code compiles, or that an emitted tool call is safe to execute?
